body: He arrives at the church in Newark twelve minutes late, because the parking on that street is what it is, and a woman at the welcome table hands him a service sheet and a warm smile. The sheet is in Spanish. She did it kindly and she did it deliberately — she saw him come in, made a decision, and reached for the pile she thought would help. He looks at it. He can read most of it if he is patient, the way anybody can read a related language on paper, and he can sing almost none of it, because the vowels do not go where his mouth expects. He says obrigado and holds it face down on his knee for an hour.

Nothing there was rude and nothing there was corrected. That is precisely why it keeps happening. The kindest possible version of the flattening is still the flattening, and the man on the chair with the sheet face down is the one who absorbs it.

Latin America gets treated as one market with one language and a footnote. Brazilian material is folded into a Spanish-language schedule on the reasoning, never stated out loud, that the words look similar written down.

They look similar written down and that is where the resemblance stops being useful. They are separate languages with separate literatures, and mutual intelligibility in speech is markedly poorer than the page leads people to expect — the nasal vowels, the reduction of unstressed syllables and the rhythm of the thing put it much further from Spanish spoken than Spanish printed. For a radio station, though, the linguistics are the smaller half of the problem. The musical traditions are not close. Brazilian worship carries a rhythmic and harmonic inheritance of its own — bossa, samba, the whole line of Brazilian popular music with its unusually sophisticated relationship to harmony, and sertanejo underneath it all — and none of that appears in Spanish-language worship from anywhere else, because it did not come from anywhere else.

The band carries 40 international stations across 29 languages, and the rule is one frequency to one language, with no station standing in for another. Familia Inspire holds HM 320.30 in Spanish and is on air. Jubilee Prayers in Portuguese holds HM 351.10, assigned and not yet opened.

Holding two Portuguese frequencies rather than one is expensive, and the expense is exactly the kind a schedule would like back. Two catalogues, two rotations, two sets of programming decisions, for a language that a spreadsheet would happily consolidate into a single number with a note about regional variation. It is kept anyway, because the alternative is what the whole industry already does — treat an entirely separate musical tradition, and a language routinely treated as a regional accent, as a rounding error inside somebody else’s schedule. Once that sentence is said out loud it stops being defensible, and it was never defensible. It was only cheap.

The habit is not confined to radio and it is not anybody’s bad intention. It comes from the way categories get built by people who have never had to listen closely. Somebody drew a box called Latin America because it was useful at the scale they worked at, and the box has been inherited ever since by people who never checked what was inside it. A conference sets up a Hispanic track and puts the Brazilians in it. A publisher licenses a worship album into Spanish and considers Portuguese covered. None of it is malice and all of it produces one result: a very large body of music treated as a dialect of a body of music it is not related to.

So the dial does the obvious thing and gives each one a number. Brasil Inspire relays from São Paulo, from Newark and from Miami — São Paulo because that is the centre of Brazilian evangelical broadcasting, Newark because the Ironbound is the densest Brazilian community in the United States, Miami for the Florida corridor. Portugal Inspire is a different station with different towers and a different repertoire, and neither of them is the other one with an accent applied.
That last point is the one people find hardest, and it is worth slowing down for. It is not about national pride.

The consolidation argument is real and it is fair to state it at its strongest. Broadcasting is a business of scale, splitting an audience halves the resources available to each half, and a single Portuguese frequency would carry twice the catalogue, twice the rotation depth and twice the reason for anybody to make it good. A listener in Lisbon can understand a singer from Belo Horizonte perfectly well. Nobody would be excluded and nobody insulted. What that argument cannot answer is what a shared station would play, because a rotation is not a language — it is a repertoire, a set of songs a congregation already knows, and the two congregations do not know the same songs. A merged frequency does not serve both. It serves whichever is larger and lets the other listen in.
Two countries can share a language and still not share a hymn book.

She grew up in Porto and has lived in London nine years, and the only Portuguese-language congregation within reach of her flat is Brazilian. She goes, because the alternative is English, and English is fine for the sermon and no good at all for the singing. Every word from the front is comprehensible and she follows the prayers without effort. Then the band starts and the room lifts, and she is standing there with the words on the screen in her own language, reading them for the first time, half a beat behind everybody, at a tempo she would not have chosen. She is not excluded from anything. She is only the one person in the building reading rather than remembering, and she has been for nine years.
That is the whole case for two frequencies, and it has nothing to do with whether she can understand the words. She can. What she does not have is a repertoire, and worship runs on repertoire.

There is an honest cost to splitting, and the smaller station pays it. Portugal Inspire serves a far smaller listenership than Brasil Inspire does, its catalogue is thinner, and a purely commercial reading of the dial would say the frequency is not earning its place. That reading is not stupid. On any measure of reach it is correct, and it would be correct next year as well.

Which is exactly why the number is held permanently rather than allocated on merit. A frequency assigned by size is a frequency that gets taken away when the size changes, and a tradition that can be outvoted off the dial was never really on it. The point of one language to one number is that the small station is not a tenant of the large one. The congregational repertoire of Lisbon and Porto does not have to justify its existence against São Paulo’s every quarter, and the woman reading the screen half a beat late has somewhere that is hers rather than somewhere she is welcome.

So Brasil holds its own frequency and Portugal holds another, with separate hosts, separate catalogues and separate schedules, because they carry different repertoires rather than one accent. The alternative was to treat an enormous nation and an entire separate musical tradition as a variant spelling, which is what usually happens, and which nobody would defend if they were made to say it in a sentence.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Both numbers are live and you can hear the difference this afternoon. HM 321.50 is Portugal Inspire — European Portuguese worship, the Lisbon and Porto congregational tradition, with Louvor da Manhã at seven in the morning and Adoração da Noite at eight in the evening. Put it on for ten minutes and then move up the dial, and the argument of this article stops being an argument and becomes something you can simply hear: two stations, one language, and repertoires that have almost nothing in common.

Then stay at HM 321.90 — Brasil Inspire (Português), hosted by Santiago Inspire and relayed from São Paulo, Newark and Miami. It carries sertanejo gospel, MPB worship and contemporary Brazilian praise, with Manhã Brasil at eight in the morning and Noite Brasileira at eight at night. It is the frequency this article exists to point at, because it is the one that is normally not given: a schedule written in Brazil for Brazilians rather than a Spanish-language rotation with a few Portuguese tracks conceded to it. If you have ever been handed the wrong service sheet by somebody being kind, this is the station that does not do that.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card — open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays. It is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else there. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Put HM 321.90 on this evening and leave it running through the cooking and the washing up, and do not treat it as a sample of a category. It is not a Latin station and it is not a Spanish station with different vowels. It is one country singing in its own language, at its own tempo, out of its own memory — and the surest way to stop flattening something is to spend an ordinary evening listening to how little it sounds like the thing you were told it was.
